paras: The Big Sandy railroad regulators were a gang in Carter County, Kentucky, led by the brothers David and William Patton, who in the summer of 1881 were reported to be driving workmen off the Big Sandy railroad. On 20 July 1881 the county judge asked Governor Blackburn for help, and the governor sent a general to the scene and offered rewards for the brothers' capture. One wire report described the workmen as "colored" and said several had been killed and others whipped, but the fuller dispatch carried by most papers named no race and no deaths.

According to a Frankfort dispatch of 20 July, the Patton brothers had been "at the head of a gang of regulators" that was "in the habit of driving off workmen on the Big Sandy railroad." The leader's alias was printed variously as Bob, "Dub," "Hub" and Rube Patton, and the Chicago Tribune gave his first name as Daniel.

The fuller version of the dispatch said the gang had threatened the contractors on the line and their employes. Several days before the dispatch, one railroad employe was robbed and then shot "to prevent his appearing against them"; the reports do not say whether he survived. A separate National Associated Press brief from Frankfort went further, stating that the regulators had been "driving colored workmen from railroads" and that "several have been killed and others whipped by the scoundrels." No victim is named in any report, and no number of dead is given.

On the morning of 20 July the Carter County judge applied to the governor for aid in quelling the disturbance. Governor Blackburn sent Gen. Nuckols (printed also as Muckoles and Muckholes) to the scene, said he would order out troops if necessary, and offered a reward of $250 each for the capture of the Pattons. The National Associated Press brief said simply that the governor "will send troops"; no report found shows that troops went or that either brother was captured.

Early in August, dispatches from Mt. Sterling and Cincinnati reported that fifteen regulators had ridden into Grayson, in Carter County, and tried to take control of the town. The town marshal raised a posse that killed three of the regulators and captured four, though the Savannah Morning News printed the dead as "thirty." None of these reports names the Pattons or mentions the railroad, so whether the Grayson raiders were the same gang is not shown.

The story reached readers through two wire versions dated Frankfort, 20 July, and ran the next day in Omaha, St. Paul, Chicago and Washington. The Omaha Daily Bee's short item, headed "Calling for Troops," was the only one to identify the workmen as Black, and it alone reported deaths and whippings. The Chicago Tribune placed the fuller dispatch under "Criminal News" as "Kentucky Outlaws," with a deck saying the governor had been asked "to Assist in Regulating Regulators," while the St. Paul Daily Globe headed it "State Authority Interposed."

A week later the dispatch reappeared in weekly digests, among them the "Record of Crime" column of the Morris Tribune and the Worthington Advance in Minnesota and the news columns of the Russellville Democrat in Arkansas. These versions treated the affair as a matter of Kentucky lawlessness and state authority, calling the gang "roughs" and "ruffians," and did not mention the race of the workmen.

The racial character of the episode and its death toll rest on the National Associated Press brief alone, which said the workmen were "colored" and that several were killed. The longer dispatch printed by the Globe, the Tribune, the National Republican and the Russellville Democrat neither confirms nor denies those details, reporting only threats, the driving off of workmen, and the shooting of one employe.

bases: An organized gang of 'regulators' led by two named brothers habitually drove workmen off a railroad construction line, with threats, a shooting, and (in one report) killings and whippings (A1, A2, A3).

Two wire services from Frankfort (National Associated Press in A1; the dispatch in A2, A3, A4, A7) agree that the Carter County judge sought the governor's aid against regulators driving off railroad workmen, but only A1 says the workmen were 'colored' and that several were killed and others whipped.

framing.detail: The Omaha Bee headed its brief 'Calling for Troops' and called the regulators 'the scoundrels'.
The Chicago Tribune ran it under 'Criminal News' as 'Kentucky Outlaws', with the deck 'The Governor of Kentucky Asked to Assist in Regulating Regulators', and called the gang 'roughs'.

The St. Paul Globe ('State Authority Interposed'), the National Republican and the Russellville Democrat printed the dispatch without comment; Minnesota weeklies carried it a week later in a 'Record of Crime' column.
